title: Pharmacognosy and Phytotherapy
description: Natural sources of drugs, classes of plant secondary metabolites, evaluation and standardisation of crude drugs, and Nigerian medicinal plants and herbal medicine regulation.

topics.title: Scope of Pharmacognosy and Evaluation of Crude Drugs
topics.summary: Definitions, collection and preparation of crude drugs, and methods of evaluation.

notes.b: Pharmacognosy (Greek pharmakon 'drug' + gnosis 'knowledge'; term coined by Seydler, 1815) is the study of drugs of natural origin — plants, animals, microbes and minerals. Crude drugs are unprocessed natural materials (leaves, bark, roots, seeds, resins). Quality depends on correct identification, time and method of collection, drying (to prevent enzymatic and microbial degradation), storage and freedom from adulteration. Ethnobotany studies how people use plants; bioprospecting searches nature for new drugs.
k: Crude drugs are unprocessed natural materials

notes.b: Evaluation confirms identity, purity and quality: organoleptic (colour, odour, taste, texture), microscopic (e.g. stomata types, trichomes, calcium oxalate crystals, starch grains; stomatal number and palisade ratio), physical (ash values — total, acid-insoluble; moisture content; extractive values; swelling index), chemical (identity tests, assays) and biological (bioassays). Chromatographic fingerprinting (TLC, HPLC) standardises herbal products. Adulteration may be accidental or deliberate substitution with inferior or spurious material.

topics.title: Alkaloids
topics.summary: Properties, tests and important medicinal alkaloids.

notes.b: Alkaloids are basic nitrogen-containing compounds, usually heterocyclic, with marked physiological activity. They are generally bitter, form water-soluble salts with acids, and are extracted by acid–base methods. General precipitating reagents include Dragendorff's (orange-red precipitate), Mayer's (cream), Wagner's (reddish-brown) and Hager's (yellow). They are classified by ring system: tropane, quinoline, isoquinoline, indole, purine, steroidal alkaloids, etc.

Morphine and codeine (isoquinoline; Papaver somniferum latex — opium) — analgesics. Quinine (quinoline; Cinchona bark) — antimalarial; quinidine — antiarrhythmic. Atropine and hyoscine (tropane; Atropa belladonna, Datura) — antimuscarinic. Reserpine (indole; Rauwolfia vomitoria — found in Nigeria) — antihypertensive. Vincristine and vinblastine (indole; Catharanthus roseus, Madagascar periwinkle) — anticancer. Caffeine (purine; coffee, tea, kola nut — Cola nitida). Physostigmine (Physostigma venenosum, the Calabar bean from south-eastern Nigeria) — anticholinesterase. Emetine (ipecacuanha) and ephedrine (Ephedra) are other examples.

topics.title: Glycosides, Tannins and Volatile Oils
topics.summary: Cardiac, anthraquinone, cyanogenic and saponin glycosides, tannins and essential oils.

notes.b: Glycosides consist of a sugar (glycone) linked to a non-sugar aglycone. Cardiac glycosides (digoxin from Digitalis lanata, digitoxin from D. purpurea; also Strophanthus) have a steroid nucleus with a lactone ring and inhibit the Na+/K+-ATPase; Keller–Kiliani and Legal/Kedde tests detect them. Anthraquinone glycosides (senna, cascara, aloe) are stimulant laxatives, detected by Borntrager's test (pink/red in ammonia). Cyanogenic glycosides (e.g. linamarin in cassava) release hydrogen cyanide; improper cassava processing causes konzo and tropical ataxic neuropathy. Saponins (e.g. from Dioscorea yams — diosgenin, a steroid precursor) froth in water and haemolyse red cells. Flavonoids (e.g. rutin, quercetin) are antioxidants.

Tannins are polyphenols that precipitate proteins; they are astringent (used in diarrhoea and wound healing) and give a blue-black or green colour with ferric chloride. Hydrolysable tannins (gallotannins) differ from condensed tannins (proanthocyanidins). Volatile (essential) oils are mixtures of terpenes and phenylpropanoids, obtained by steam distillation, with antiseptic, carminative and aromatic uses: eucalyptus oil (cineole), peppermint oil (menthol), clove oil (eugenol — dental analgesic), lemongrass (citral; Cymbopogon citratus, common in Nigeria), and Ocimum gratissimum ('scent leaf', effirin/nchanwu/daidoya).

topics.title: Nigerian Medicinal Plants
topics.summary: Important indigenous plants, their constituents and evidence for use.

notes.b: Azadirachta indica (neem, 'dogoyaro') — antimalarial folk use, insecticidal limonoids (azadirachtin). Vernonia amygdalina (bitter leaf, 'ewuro', 'onugbu', 'shiwaka') — sesquiterpene lactones; traditional antimalarial and antidiabetic use. Moringa oleifera — highly nutritious leaves (protein, vitamins A and C, iron, calcium). Garcinia kola (bitter kola, 'orogbo', 'akuilu') — biflavonoids (kolaviron) with antioxidant and hepatoprotective activity. Xylopia aethiopica (Ethiopian pepper, 'eeru', 'uda') — postpartum use. Allium sativum (garlic) — allicin, antimicrobial and lipid-lowering. Zingiber officinale (ginger) — gingerols, antiemetic. Aloe vera — wound healing and laxative. Hibiscus sabdariffa (zobo) — anthocyanins, mild antihypertensive. Cajanus cajan (pigeon pea) — studied for antisickling activity; Niprisan (NIPRD's herbal antisickling product) is a Nigerian example.

Traditional use suggests leads but efficacy and safety must be proven by pharmacological and clinical studies. Herbal products can be toxic (e.g. hepatotoxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids, nephrotoxic aristolochic acid), contaminated (heavy metals, microbes, adulteration with undeclared drugs such as steroids or sildenafil), variable in content, and can interact with orthodox drugs (e.g. St John's wort induces CYP3A4; garlic and ginkgo increase bleeding risk with warfarin). The Nigerian Institute for Pharmaceutical Research and Development (NIPRD, Abuja) researches phytomedicines.

topics.title: Herbal Medicine Regulation and Extraction Methods
topics.summary: Extraction techniques, standardisation, and regulation of herbal medicines in Nigeria.

notes.b: Extraction separates active constituents from plant material using solvents. Methods: maceration (soaking at room temperature), percolation (solvent passes slowly through a packed drug), infusion (short soaking in hot water, e.g. teas), decoction (boiling in water — suitable for hard, heat-stable materials like roots and bark), Soxhlet (continuous hot extraction with a recycling solvent), and modern methods (ultrasound-assisted, microwave-assisted, supercritical CO2). Solvent choice depends on polarity: water and alcohols extract polar compounds (glycosides, tannins); hexane and petroleum ether extract non-polar compounds (fats, some terpenes).

In Nigeria, NAFDAC registers herbal medicines and related products, requiring evidence of safety, quality (good manufacturing practice, microbial and heavy metal limits) and appropriate labelling; herbal products may be 'listed' with evidence of safety before full registration with efficacy data. WHO guidelines cover good agricultural and collection practices (GACP) for medicinal plants and the integration of traditional medicine into health systems. Pharmacists should ask patients about herbal medicine use, report adverse reactions and counsel on interactions.
